question_text: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents for a well-child examination. The boy was born at term via vaginal delivery and has been healthy except for impaired vision due to severe short-sightedness. He is at the 97th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. Oral examination shows a high-arched palate. He has abnormally long, slender fingers and toes, and his finger joints are hyperflexible. The patient is asked to place his thumbs in the palms of the same hand and then clench to form a fist. The thumbs are noted to protrude beyond the ulnar border of the hand. Slit lamp examination shows lens subluxation in the superotemporal direction bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

                    ### Question
                    A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents for a well-child examination. The boy was born at term via vaginal delivery and has been healthy except for impaired vision due to severe short-sightedness. He is at the 97th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. Oral examination shows a high-arched palate. He has abnormally long, slender fingers and toes, and his finger joints are hyperflexible. The patient is asked to place his thumbs in the palms of the same hand and then clench to form a fist. The thumbs are noted to protrude beyond the ulnar border of the hand. Slit lamp examination shows lens subluxation in the superotemporal direction bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Mutation in fibrillin-1 gene
opb. Defective collagen cross-linking
opc. Nondisjunction of sex chromosomes
opd. Mutation of the FMR1 gene
ope. Mutation in RET gene

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of the 3-year-old boy, including severe myopia, high-arched palate, long slender fingers, hyperflexible joints, and lens subluxation, is consistent with Marfan syndrome, a connective tissue disorder. The underlying cause of Marfan syndrome is a mutation in the fibrillin-1 gene, which is responsible for the structural integrity of connective tissues. The reasoning chains correctly identify these features and link them to the mutation in the fibrillin-1 gene, supported by the evidence that lens subluxation is a common manifestation of Marfan syndrome. Other options, such as defective collagen cross-linking, nondisjunction of sex chromosomes, mutation of the FMR1 gene, and mutation in the RET gene, do not align with the specific features presented in this case.
